name: Belgian Golden Strong Ale
title: Belgian Golden Strong Ale: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Belgian golden strong ale explained: pale, bone-dry, fizzy and deceptively strong, plus how to serve it and Indian dishes to pair.
tagline: Looks like a lager, drinks like champagne, and is often nearly as strong as wine. Respect it.
tastes:
The golden strong ale is a trick played on the eye. It looks pale and bright, like a pilsner, but it can be as strong as a light wine. The style took its modern shape around 1970, when Duvel Moortgat turned its strong ale pale to answer the fashion for golden lager: very light pilsner malt, a good dose of plain sugar to thin the body, and a vigorous Belgian yeast.

The sugar is the secret. It ferments away completely, so the beer finishes very dry and light despite all that alcohol. Pear, apple and a little citrus come from the yeast, along with a peppery spice. The hops are more noticeable than in a blonde, adding a fine bitterness and a herbal or spicy note that keeps the finish crisp. Carbonation is high, sometimes close to sparkling wine. It is less sweet than a tripel, though the two are close cousins and many drinkers confuse them.

profile.look: Pale straw to deep gold, brilliantly clear, with a huge, rocky white head that lasts.
profile.aroma_flavour: Pear, apple and citrus from the yeast, peppery spice, a soft pale malt base and a clean herbal hop note.
profile.mouthfeel: Light body for its strength, very high carbonation, bone-dry and warming at the finish.
profile.ingredients: Pilsner malt, a large share of plain white sugar, Saaz or Styrian Golding type hops, a highly attenuative Belgian yeast.

in_india: This is a beer to share, not a summer session drink. In Indian heat its lightness tempts you to drink it like lager, which at eight or nine per cent is a mistake. It makes a good alternative to sparkling wine at a wedding or anniversary, poured into tulips in small measures. Few Indian brewers make one, as it needs a strong, healthy yeast and careful fermentation control. Imported bottles turn up in premium shops; check the date and buy cold.

pairings.why: High carbonation and dryness clean the palate after every rich, spiced mouthful of rice.
The light, spongy Gujarati snack meets bright fruit and fizz in an easy vegetarian match.
Dry, peppery beer cuts the sour, spicy pickle-style prawns without being swamped.
The beer's crisp dryness balances the dense cashew sweetness of the barfi.
